# Server-server API

`Async::Matrix::ServerServer::Server` is the federation client: a resource rooted at another
homeserver, with a navigator per concept the specification names and a representation per answer.

```ruby
require "async/matrix"

key = Async::Matrix::ServerKey.load("/etc/synapse/signing.key")

Async::Matrix::ServerServer::Server.open("https://matrix.example.com") do |unsigned|
  server = unsigned.signed_as("example.com", key, "matrix.example.com")

  puts unsigned.server_version.get_version.name
  puts server.query.query_profile("@alice:matrix.example.com").displayname

  # A join is a template to sign and send back:
  template = server.joins_v1.make_join(room_id, "@bob:example.com", versions: ["11"])
end
```

## Signing

There is no access token. A server proves who it is by signing the request, so
`Async::Matrix::Middleware::Signed` sits below the resource and signs the method, the path, the
origin, the destination and the body as a document. The signature is over the canonical form rather
than over the bytes, so it cannot depend on how the sender wrote them.

`Async::Matrix::ServerKey` reads the one line a homeserver keeps its ed25519 key in, and is what
the other side fetches from `/_matrix/key/v2/server` to check a signature against.

Some endpoints are not signed at all. The version, the keys, the discovery document and the OpenID
exchange are read before there is anything to sign with, so they are asked for through the unsigned
resource.

## Answers which are not JSON

`/media/download` answers `multipart/mixed`: a document describing the file, and then the file, or
a `Location` pointing at it. `Async::Matrix::Wrapper::Multipart` reads both, so
`Async::Matrix::ServerServer::FederatedContent` has bytes and a description rather than a body to
parse.

The first versions of `send_join` and `send_invite` answered `[200, {...}]` — a status beside the
body — which the second versions replaced with the body alone. Those representations read either
shape.

## Events

Since room version 3 an event ID is the hash of its redacted form rather than a field it carries,
so a representation reads events by type rather than looking one up by ID.

A join, a leave and a knock are all built by the server which has the room: it answers a
`MembershipTemplate` for the asking server to hash, sign and send back, because only it knows the
state the event should point at.

## Withdrawals

v1.18 dropped the first versions of `send_join` and `send_leave`, so those layers register the
withdrawal and the methods say what replaced them:

```ruby
Async::Matrix::ServerServer::Server["v1.19"].open(url) do |server|
  server.joins_v1.send_join_v1(room_id, event_id, event)
  # => Async::Matrix::RemovedOperationError: #send_join_v1 was removed in v1.18: call #send_join_v2 instead!
end
```

## Testing it

The suite signs as the homeserver it is testing, using the key checked into `synapse/`: a
homeserver verifies a signature made by its own server name against the key it already holds rather
than fetching one, so every authenticated endpoint is reachable from a single server. There is no
other way to do it — a server name invented by the suite would have no keys for anybody to fetch.

```shell
bin/test --keep-alive --api server-server
```
